questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Being able to take courses that I couldn't take at home, and getting an interesting cultural experience.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy, the International Student and Scholar Services had put great effort into holding zoom lectures and giving us relevant information. They are also very responsive throughout the semester if you need any help.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had trouble paying for the mandatory health insurance, as their system did not support all the characters in my name, leading to my card constantly being declined. So I needed help figuring out how to pay in person.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Very difficult. Applying for on campus housing is not worth it as it is very competitive and has a $50 fee just to apply. Off campus is very competitive with most UT students already securing housing for the entire school year, at the start of the previous school year, so more than a year in advance. From what I have heard from other exchange students, the easiest is definitely to find a housing co-op. If you rent at a corporate landlord, try and find somewhere where you can pay for utilities through the landlord, as starting service with the City of Austin Utilities is quite cumbersome, and it is quite an ordeal to try and get back the deposit.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: If you are going to buy groceries and cook for yourself, there are not a lot of options around campus. There is a food co-op and target, which are fine but have limited options. For a more substantial supermarket, similar to Føtex or Meny, go to H-E-B. The easiest H-E-B to get to from campus is one south of downtown, as there is a bus that goes directly there from west campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: For CS students, once accepted for the exchange program you have to apply to have CS as your major. The CS department only guarantees you to have 2 CS courses, and you need to send them a list of courses you are interested in taking. Shortly before the registration opens you will have a zoom meeting with your academic advisor, who will tell you which 2 CS courses you will get, and then you talk about what other courses you want. I took Electrical and Computer Engineering courses, even though they are often restricted to engineering students, I solved this by my advisor giving me the email address for the ECE department advisor, who then gave me the courses I was interested in.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Your advisor can help you figure out which courses you can take, and explain how to register for courses.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was very successful. I got all of the courses I was interested in, even managing to circumvent the restrictions on engineering courses, by just asking the relevant advisor.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Talk with your assigned advisor, and if you want to take courses in other departments, get the relevant advisors email address from your advisor.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I found that the courses were a similar difficulty as courses at UCPH. I have heard from other exchange students in law, business and humanities, that they have found the courses here to be quite easy. But I found that science and engineering courses were about the same difficulty as at home.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Quite similar with two lectures a week and assignments every week or every other week, depending on the course. There were two major differences from UCPH. The first being that we here have 4 courses at a time, while the block schedule at UCPH means we only have 2 courses at a time. The other major difference is that the US university system has midterm exams in all courses, and quite a lot of them. One of the courses I had, had 3 midterms and one final exam, meaning one exam every month.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: C S 360V Virtualization, C S 358H Introduction to Quantum Information Science, ECE 302 Introduction to Electrical Engineering, ECE 316 Digital Logic Design.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
C S 360V I found to be quite easy and straightforward, and reasonably interesting, I think it is a good course that also allows you to have free time.
C S 358H I found to be quite difficult to understand, and not as interesting as I had hoped. If you want to take it, you should definitely prepare by doing linear algebra and getting comfortable with calculating with complex numbers.
ECE 302 is notoriously difficult, and definitely not a course you want to take with other difficult courses. But if you are interested in learning about circuits and transistors it is a great course.
ECE 316 is awesome. I thought it was a straightforward course that wasn't too difficult, and also quite interesting. For the lab assignments you get to program FPGA's.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Nothing, I think on average things are about as expensive as in Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are lots of recreational sports and cultural clubs on campus. There are sports games in different sports, most notably of course being the American football games. The RecSports Outdoors Center also organizes hiking/biking/canoeing trips to different parts of Texas and neighboring states.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go on trips with the Outdoors Center, it is a great opportunity to meet other exchange- and local- students, as well as getting to explore Texas.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: There are quite a few museums on campus that you have free access to with your student ID if you've got nothing else planned. Barton Springs Creek, Zilker Park, and the trails around Lady Bird Lake, in downtown, are also all great places to go hang out or go for a walk. The Texas capitol building is also pretty cool to see, and it is free to visit.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, UT and Austin are both quite cosmopolitan, so if you know how things work in America I don't think there will be much of a shock.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Talk with the people you have courses with.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I don't know, it's America, so I think it's pretty similar to most western countries in many ways.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Go on tours with the outdoors center.
2. Don't take too difficult courses so you can have time to go explore.
3. Explore campus and all the different events happening on and around it.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you are in humanities, depending on your specific field of study, or if you are LGBTQ, you might want to reconsider going to UT. As the newly appointed president of the university is kind of a political appointee, and has previously worked for the republican party in Texas. There currently rumors that the humanities are going to be heavily limited, with some fields of study expected to be scrapped, and a lot of courses no longer being offered going forward. Additionally, while I was here, fall 2025, the Trump administration invited a number of universities to sign a "compact" that would effectively put the university under the presidents control, and UT was the only university to not reject the compact. At time of writing, the deadline for signing the compact has passed, with UT neither accepting or rejecting it.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to take courses I can't take at home.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The constant midterms.

questions.answer: Yes
